result:
The proposed answer of 1/8 is incorrect. The correct limit is 1/10.

**Setup.** Identify each 2-subset $\{i,j\}$ with the grid point $(i,j)$, $1\le i<j\le n$. Two vertices are adjacent exactly when they differ by a unit step in one coordinate, so $T_2(P_n)$ is the induced subgraph of the square grid on the staircase region $\{1\le i<j\le n\}$. It has $N=\binom{n}{2}\sim n^2/2$ vertices and maximum degree 4.

**Lower bound.** A vertex dominates at most $\Delta+1=5$ vertices, so $\gamma \ge N/5 \sim n^2/10$.

**Upper bound.** $\mathbb{Z}^2$ has a perfect dominating set of density $1/5$, for example $\{(i,j): i+2j \equiv 0 \pmod 5\}$. Restrict this pattern to the region. Vertices near the staircase boundary may be left undominated, but the boundary has only $O(n)$ vertices, so adding them to the dominating set costs $O(n)$. Hence $\gamma \le n^2/10 + O(n)$.

Combining the two bounds gives $\gamma(T_2(P_n))/n^2 \to 1/10$.

The proposed argument also fails internally. It recognizes the $1/5$ density and the $N\sim n^2/2$ count, then abandons the $1/10$ prediction in favour of an unexplained "observed" $n^2/8$ fitted to tiny cases. Small-$n$ data cannot establish an asymptotic constant that the lower bound already rules out: $1/8 > 1/10$ is not contradicted by a lower bound, but the upper bound above shows $1/8$ is not attained. The $n^2/8$ fit is not supported.

VERDICT: REJECT

CONFIDENCE: 5
